title: Car Setup and Tuning
intro: Setup is the adjustment of a car to a track, to the conditions and to the driver. In a real team it is done by engineers with the driver's feedback; in a racing game the player does it in the tuning menu, with the same adjustments and the same effects, provided the game models them. A good setup does not make a car faster than its grip allows. It makes the grip usable: a car that is balanced and predictable lets the driver go closer to the limit in every corner.

blocks.text: How to set up a car

items: Start from a known baseline: the default or a recommended setup for the car and track.
Drive enough laps to be consistent before changing anything; a driver who varies by half a second cannot judge a setup change worth a tenth.

Describe the problem precisely: which corners, which phase (entry, mid-corner or exit), slow or fast corners, and whether the front or the rear slides first (see understeer and oversteer on #/racing/vehicle-dynamics).
Change one thing at a time, by a clear step, and note the result. If it did not help, put it back.
Fix the biggest problem first. Small refinements cannot rescue a car that is badly unbalanced.
Fix the driving before the car: a car that understeers on entry may just be braking too late.
Compound: softer tyres grip more but wear faster and can overheat; harder ones last longer. Many series and games offer several compounds plus intermediate and full wet tyres for rain.
Hot pressure: set the cold pressure so the pressure is right once the tyre is at temperature. Too high shrinks the contact patch and makes the car skate; too low makes it lazy and overheats the tyre.

Temperature across the tread: measured at the inside, middle and outside edges after a run. A hot middle means too much pressure; hot edges, too little. A tyre usually works best with its inside edge a little hotter than its outside, which tells you the camber is about right.

Camber is the tilt of the wheel seen from the front. Negative camber (top of the wheel leaning in) keeps the tyre flatter on the road when the car rolls in a corner, which adds cornering grip. Too much reduces the contact patch under braking and acceleration and wears the inside edge.

Toe is whether the wheels point in or out, seen from above. Front toe-out sharpens the turn-in but makes the car wander on the straight. Rear toe-in makes the rear more stable, at the cost of a little drag and tyre wear.
Caster is the backward tilt of the steering axis. More caster gives stronger self-centring, more steering weight and more camber gain as the wheels are turned. Often fixed in race cars and games.

blocks.text: Springs, anti-roll bars and ride height

Springs hold the car up and control how much it pitches and rolls. Anti-roll bars (sway bars) link the left and right wheels so they resist roll without stiffening the car over single bumps. The key rule: the end of the car that is stiffer in roll takes a bigger share of the cornering load transfer, and because of load sensitivity that end loses grip first. So a stiffer front makes the car understeer more, and a stiffer rear makes it oversteer more. Anti-roll bars are the quickest way to adjust balance.

items: Stiffer overall: quicker response and a more stable aerodynamic platform, but less grip over bumps and kerbs.
Softer overall: more mechanical grip on bumpy tracks and in slow corners, but more roll and pitch, and a lazier response.

Ride height: lower lowers the centre of mass (less load transfer) and, on a car with a shaped floor, adds downforce, until the car hits the ground or the floor stalls. Raising the rear relative to the front (more rake) generally moves aerodynamic balance forward.

blocks.text: Dampers (shock absorbers) control how fast the suspension moves, so they set how quickly weight transfers, not how much. Bump (compression) damping resists the wheel moving up; rebound damping resists it moving back down. Because they act during the transition, dampers tune the car's behaviour on entry and exit: for example, more front rebound slows the weight leaving the front tyres when the driver gets on the throttle, which can reduce exit understeer. Many dampers have separate slow-speed settings (for body movement: braking, roll) and fast-speed settings (for bumps and kerbs).

items: Wing angle: more wing is more downforce and more drag. Add it for tracks with many fast corners; take it off for tracks with long straights.

Aero balance: more front wing (or less rear) moves grip forward and makes the car oversteer more in fast corners; more rear wing makes it more stable at speed. Because downforce grows with speed, aero changes mostly affect fast corners, while mechanical changes (springs, bars) mostly affect slow ones.
A car can be well balanced in slow corners and badly balanced in fast ones, or the reverse; fix the slow corners with mechanical setup and the fast ones with aero.

blocks.text: A differential lets the left and right driven wheels turn at different speeds in a corner. An open differential sends drive to whichever wheel spins easiest, so the unloaded inside wheel spins away the power. A limited-slip differential (LSD) partly locks the two wheels together.

items: Acceleration lock (power side): more locking puts down more power out of slow corners, but resists the car turning, giving understeer on exit, and if the rear does break loose it goes more suddenly.
Deceleration lock (coast side): more locking makes the car more stable under braking and on entry but less willing to turn in.
Preload: a base amount of locking at all times. More preload makes the car more stable and predictable but more reluctant to turn at low speed.
Common types are named for when they lock: a 1-way locks only under power, a 2-way locks equally under power and braking, a 1.5-way in between.

blocks.text: The final drive ratio scales all the gears together; individual ratios set each gear. Shorter (numerically higher) gearing gives harder acceleration and a lower top speed. A common rule is to set the final drive so the car just reaches the rev limiter in top gear at the end of the longest straight, allowing a little extra for a slipstream in a race. Individual ratios are then spaced so that the car comes out of each important corner in a gear that keeps the engine in its power band.

items: Brake bias (balance) is the share of braking force at the front. Because weight moves forward under braking, the front tyres can take most of it, typically 55 to 70 percent. More front bias makes the car stable but understeer on entry and risks locking the fronts; more rear bias helps the car rotate but risks locking the rears and spinning.
Brake pressure: in some cars and games the overall pedal force can be scaled, which mainly changes how the pedal feels to the driver.
Brake cooling: too little and the brakes overheat and fade; too much and they stay too cold to bite well, and add drag.

blocks.text: Balance of performance, ballast and fuel

In GT and touring car classes, organisers equalise different car models with balance of performance (BoP): extra weight, smaller air restrictors or power limits for the faster cars. Some series also add success ballast to the winners of earlier races. Many games copy this in their racing classes or by a performance rating that limits which cars may enter. A full fuel tank adds weight too, which is why a car gets faster as it burns fuel through a stint.

items: Understeer on entry: move brake bias rearward, soften the front anti-roll bar, add front toe-out, reduce coast-side diff lock, or brake earlier and more smoothly.
Understeer mid-corner: soften the front (springs or anti-roll bar) or stiffen the rear; in fast corners add front wing or take off rear wing.
Understeer on exit: reduce power-side diff lock, add front rebound damping, soften the rear, or wait longer for the throttle.
Oversteer on entry: move brake bias forward, add coast-side diff lock, add rear toe-in, or trail brake less aggressively.
Oversteer on exit (power oversteer): soften the rear springs or anti-roll bar, use a higher gear, or apply the throttle more progressively.
Unstable at high speed: add rear wing or reduce rake.
Slow on the straights but fast in corners: take off wing, or lengthen the gearing.

blocks.text: These rules describe the usual direction of each change, not a law. Suspension geometry, tyres and aerodynamics interact, so a change can behave differently on another car. Test every change on track.

Sources: Smith, C. (1978), Tune to Win, Aero Publishers. Milliken, W. F. and Milliken, D. L. (1995), Race Car Vehicle Dynamics, SAE International, chapters 16 to 19 on suspension and the differential. Staniforth, A. (2006), Competition Car Suspension, 4th ed., Haynes. Haney, P. and Braun, J. (1995), Inside Racing Technology, TV Motorsports.
